questions.title: Platyhelminths needing one intermediate host, except
questions.question: The following platyhelminths require one intermediate host EXCEPT ?

explanations.A: Incorrect as the EXCEPT answer. Fasciola hepatica needs only one intermediate host, a snail, before its metacercaria encysts on aquatic vegetation and infects man directly, so it belongs with the one-host group.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the EXCEPT answer. Schistosoma haematobium also needs only one intermediate host, a snail, whose cercariae then penetrate human skin directly with no second intermediate host, so it too belongs with the one-host group.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the EXCEPT answer. Fasciolopsis buski likewise needs only one intermediate host, a snail, before its metacercaria encysts on water vegetation and is swallowed by man, so it belongs with the one-host group.
explanations.D: Correct. Diphyllobothrium latum is the exception: it needs two intermediate hosts in succession, Cyclops and then a fresh-water fish, before its plerocercoid larva becomes infective to man -- unlike Fasciola hepatica, Schistosoma haematobium and Fasciolopsis buski, which all complete their pre-human development in a single snail intermediate host. This one-host-versus-two-host contrast is the mirror image of this chapter's own Q1, which asks the same question about platyhelminths needing two hosts.

questions.learning_objective: State that Diphyllobothrium latum is the exception among these platyhelminths, needing two intermediate hosts (Cyclops, then fish), unlike Fasciola hepatica, Schistosoma haematobium and Fasciolopsis buski, which each need only one (a snail).

questions.title: Cestodes not transmitted by insects
questions.question: Which of the following parasites is not transmitted by insects ?

explanations.A: Incorrect as the exception. Hymenolepis diminuta's cysticercoid larva develops in a true insect intermediate host, a grain beetle or flea, so it belongs with the insect-transmitted group.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the exception. Dipylidium caninum's cysticercoid larva likewise develops within an infected flea, a true insect, so it too belongs with the insect-transmitted group.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the exception. Guinea worm (Dracunculus medinensis) is carried by Cyclops, a small crustacean loosely grouped with arthropod vectors in basic teaching, closer to the insect-transmitted group than to Diphyllobothrium latum's route.
explanations.D: Correct. Diphyllobothrium latum's second intermediate host is a fresh-water fish, reached only after an earlier Cyclops stage -- man becomes infected by eating fish, a route with no insect or insect-like arthropod involved at the point of human infection at all, unlike Hymenolepis diminuta and Dipylidium caninum (true fleas/beetles) or Guinea worm (Cyclops, still an arthropod-adjacent vector). This distinction between fish-borne and arthropod-borne cestode transmission is what separates D. latum from the other three parasites in this list.

questions.learning_objective: State that Diphyllobothrium latum, transmitted via fish, is the exception among these parasites, unlike Hymenolepis diminuta and Dipylidium caninum (fleas/beetles) or Guinea worm (Cyclops).

questions.title: Suckers as organs of fixation
questions.question: Suckers are organs of fixation in ?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Nematodes (roundworms) attach or anchor by other means -- a mouth armed with plates or hooks, or a penetrating anterior end -- not by suckers.
explanations.B: Correct. Suckers are the organ of fixation in trematodes, which typically bear an oral and a ventral sucker, and in some cestodes, whose scolex bears four suckers (as tested elsewhere in this chapter for Taenia saginata and Taenia solium) -- though not every cestode relies on suckers alone, since Diphyllobothrium latum's scolex instead uses bothria (shallow attachment grooves). Recognising that suckers span two of the three helminth groups, not just one, is what this question tests.
explanations.C: Incorrect as a complete answer. Suckers are not confined to cestodes alone -- trematodes also rely on them, and some cestodes (Diphyllobothrium latum) use bothria instead of true suckers.
explanations.D: Incorrect as a complete answer. Suckers are not confined to trematodes alone -- most cestode scoleces, such as those of the two Taenia species, also bear suckers.

questions.learning_objective: State that suckers are the organ of fixation shared by trematodes and most (but not all) cestodes, not by nematodes.

questions.title: Cysticercosis, except
questions.question: Human infection with cysticercosis may occur in the following methods EXCEPT ?

options.A: Ingestion of pork contaminated with cysticercus cellulosae
options.B: Ingestion of food contaminated with Taenia solium egg

explanations.A: Correct. Eating pork containing cysticercus cellulosae gives man the adult worm, taeniasis, not cysticercosis -- cysticercosis (tissue larvae) instead requires man to ingest T. solium's EGGS, not its pork-borne larval cyst. This is the same distinction tested by this chapter's own Q41/Q52, and is exactly why cysticercosis, unlike taeniasis, can occur without ever eating pork at all.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the EXCEPT answer. Ingesting food contaminated with T. solium eggs is a genuine cysticercosis route -- the ingested egg's oncosphere penetrates the gut wall and disseminates to tissue, so this belongs with the true causes of cysticercosis.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the EXCEPT answer. External autoinfection -- perianal contamination with the patient's own eggs, then re-ingestion -- is a genuine route to cysticercosis in a person already carrying the adult worm, so it belongs with the true causes.
explanations.D: Incorrect as the EXCEPT answer. Internal autoinfection -- reverse peristalsis carrying gravid proglottids or eggs back into the stomach, where gastric acid frees the oncospheres -- is likewise a genuine route to cysticercosis in a T. solium carrier, so it belongs with the true causes.

questions.learning_objective: State that eating pork with cysticercus cellulosae causes taeniasis, not cysticercosis, unlike egg ingestion or external/internal autoinfection, which are the genuine cysticercosis routes.

questions.title: Cestodes characterized by
questions.question: Cestodes are characterized by ?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Cestodes do have a primitive nervous system -- a nerve ring in the scolex giving off longitudinal nerve cords along the strobila -- so this statement is false.
explanations.B: Correct. Cestodes are hermaphrodites: each proglottid carries both male and female reproductive organs, allowing self-fertilisation as well as cross-fertilisation between segments or worms. This is the same hermaphroditic body plan already established for cestodes generally in this chapter's own Q34, distinguishing them from the nematodes, which have separate sexes.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Cestodes do have an excretory system, made up of flame cells (protonephridia) draining into longitudinal excretory canals, so this statement is false.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Cestodes are flattened dorsoventrally but they are segmented, not unsegmented -- their body is divided into a chain of proglottids, the defining feature tested in this chapter's own Q34, so the "unsegmented" half of this statement is false.

questions.learning_objective: State that cestodes are hermaphroditic, unlike the false alternative statements that they lack a nervous or excretory system or are unsegmented.
